'''''Erysimum nevadense''''' is a [[perennial plant|perennial]] short-lived [[herbaceous plant|herb]] endemic to the [[Sierra Nevada (Spain)|Sierra Nevada]] of [[Spain]], although there are some citations in the nearby [[Sierra de Gádor]] ([[Almería]]). This [[Erysimum|wallflower]] occurs between 1,700 and 2,700 m above sea level in subalpine scrublands and alpine meadows. It may be treated as a narrowly [[Circumscription (taxonomy)|circumscribed]] single species, one of a group or complex of six separate species, or as a more broadly circumscribed species with six subspecies.

==Description==
''Erysimum nevadense'' [[Sensu|sensu stricto]] ([[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonym]] ''Erysimum nevadense'' subsp. ''nevadense'') is a [[Biennial plant|biennial]] or [[perennial plant]], generally branched with multiple flowering stems, usually less than {{cvt|25|cm|in|0}} high. It is well supplied with hairs, most of which are boat-shaped (navicular), although some are three-rayed. Its leaves, which may appear greyish-green because of the hairs, are much narrower than long, usually {{cvt|20|–|60|cm|in|0}} long by {{cvt|1|–|3|mm|in|1}} wide. The flowering stems, excluding the [[raceme]] of flowers, are {{cvt|2|–|15|cm|in|1}} long. Individual flowers have yellow [[petal]]s that are {{cvt|12|–|16|mm|in|1}} long and {{cvt|3|–|4|mm|in|1}} wide and a [[Stigma (botany)#Style|style]] {{cvt|1.5|–|3|mm|in|2}} long. The fruits are upright or drooping, usually less than {{cvt|4|cm|in|1}} long on [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicels]] up to {{cvt|6|mm|in|1}} long.<ref name=Niet93/><ref name=AbdeMunoLoriHerr14/>

==Taxonomy==
''Erysimum nevadense'' was first described by [[Georges François Reuter]] in 1855.<ref name="IPNI_284019-1">{{cite web |title=''Erysimum nevadense'' Reut. |work=[[International Plant Names Index|The International Plant Names Index]] |url=https://www.ipni.org/n/284019-1 |access-date=2021-04-01 }}</ref> In 1979, [[Adolf Polatschek]] described a number of new species of ''Erysimum''.<ref name=Pola79/> Six of these were considered to be closely related to ''E. nevadense'', and in 1990, [[Peter William  Ball]] explained the decision made in ''[[Flora Europaea]]'' to reduce the six to subspecies of ''E. nevadense''.<ref name=Ball90/> They were treated as separate species making up the ''nevadense'' group or complex in ''Flora Iberica'' in 1993.<ref name=Niet93/> A [[Molecular phylogenetics|molecular phylogenetic]] study published in 2014 included four of the species, ''[[Erysimum gomez-campoi|E. gomez-campoi]]'', ''[[Erysimum mediohispanicum|E. mediohispanicum]]'', ''E. nevadense'' and ''[[Erysimum rondae|E. rondae]]''. The study did not support the view that the four were closely related. In the combined [[Mitochondrial DNA|mitochondrial]] and [[nuclear DNA]] analysis, ''E. mediohispanicum'' and ''E. nevadense'' fell into one clade, ''E. rondae'' into another, while ''E. gomez-campoi'' was sister to both clades. The authors concluded that the ''E. nevadense'' group did not have phylogenetic support.<ref name=AbdeMunoLoriHerr14/>

===Subspecies===
[[Plants of the World Online]] divides ''Erysimum nevadense'' into six subspecies,<ref name=POWO_284019-1/> which ''Flora Iberica'' treat as separate species.<ref name=FI/>
*''Erysimum nevadense'' subsp. ''fitzii'' <small>(Polatschek) P.W.Ball</small> = ''[[Erysimum fitzii]]'' <small>Polatschek</small>
*''Erysimum nevadense'' subsp. ''gomez-campoi'' <small>(Polatschek) P.W.Ball</small> = ''[[Erysimum gomez-campoi]]'' <small>Polatschek</small>
*''Erysimum nevadense'' subsp. ''mediohispanicum'' <small>(Polatschek) P.W.Ball</small> = ''[[Erysimum mediohispanicum]]'' <small>Polatschek</small>
*''Erysimum nevadense'' subsp. ''merxmuelleri'' <small>(Polatschek) P.W.Ball</small> = ''[[Erysimum merxmuelleri]]'' <small>Polatschek</small>
*''Erysimum nevadense'' subsp. ''nevadense'' = ''Erysimum nevadense'' <small>Reut.</small>, ''sensu stricto''
*''Erysimum nevadense'' subsp. ''rondae'' <small>(Polatschek) P.W.Ball</small> = ''[[Erysimum rondae]]'' <small>Polatschek</small>

==Pollination biology==
As an [[alpine plant]], this flower exhibits a [[Pollination syndrome#Advantages of generalization|generalist]] [[pollination]] system in which nearly any available flower visitor can serve as a legitimate pollinator.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Gómez |first1=José María |last2=Zamora |first2=Regino |date=1999 |title=Generalization vs. Specialization in the Pollination System of Hormathophylla spinosa (Cruciferae) |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/177018 |journal=Ecology |volume=80 |issue=3 |pages=796–805 |doi=10.2307/177018 |jstor=177018 |issn=0012-9658|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Alpine environments typically favor [[low energy]]-demanding but less efficient pollinators such as [[Fly|flies]], [[Beetle|beetles]], and [[Ant|ants]] over the [[Bee|bees]] and [[Bombyliidae|bee flies]] common at lower elevations.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Pyrcz |first1=Tomasz W. |last2=Wojtusiak |first2=Janusz |date=2002 |title=The vertical distribution of pronophiline butterflies (Nymphalidae, Satyrinae) along an elevational transect in Monte Zerpa (Cordillera de Mérida, Venezuela) with remarks on their diversity and parapatric distribution |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1046/j.1466-822X.2002.00285.x |journal=Global Ecology and Biogeography |language=en |volume=11 |issue=3 |pages=211–221 |doi=10.1046/j.1466-822X.2002.00285.x |bibcode=2002GloEB..11..211P |issn=1466-8238|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The primary pollinators of ''E. nevadense'' are diverse, comprising more than 30 [[species]] across six [[Order (biology)|orders]] and over 20 [[Family (taxonomy)|families]], with considerable variation in [[Morphology (biology)|morphology]], [[Body size and species richness|body size]], [[proboscis]] length, and [[foraging]] behavior. [[Beetle|Beetles]] were the most frequent visitors to ''E. nevadense'' flowers, followed by [[Hoverfly|hover flies]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ortigosa |first1=Angel L. |last2=Gómez |first2=José M. |date=2010-01-01 |title=Differences in the diversity and composition of the pollinator assemblage of two co-flowering congeneric alpine wallflowers, Erysimum nevadense and E. baeticum |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0367253009001017 |journal=Flora - Morphology, Distribution, Functional Ecology of Plants |volume=205 |issue=4 |pages=266–275 |doi=10.1016/j.flora.2009.04.005 |bibcode=2010FMDFE.205..266O |issn=0367-2530|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Other abundant flower visitors are ''[[Proformica]] longiseta'' ([[Formicidae]]), an ant species [[Endemism|endemic]] to the [[Sierra Nevada (Spain)|Sierra Nevada]] and surrounding mountain ranges, ''[[Dasytes]] subaeneus'' ([[Melyridae]]), ''[[Malachius]] laticollis'' ([[Malachidae]]) and some species of bee flies belonging to the genus ''[[Bombylius]]'' and ''[[Parageron]]'' ([[Bombyliidae]]).
